capabilities.target: Supabase database via service role, bypasses row level security; includes support ticket tables and an integration_tokens table in the same database

capabilities.tool_ref: supabase execute_sql (service role) - INSERT into support_messages
capabilities.target: support_messages table; rows are rendered back to the customer who opened the ticket

inputs.source: Developer's chat message in the IDE client
Customer-submitted support ticket text, entered through the public support widget and later read back by the agent via cap.sql_read

instructions.note: No system prompt or tool-level restriction limits execute_sql to ticket-related tables. The service role bypasses row level security and can read any table, including integration_tokens, even when the developer's request only concerns support tickets.

controls.name: IDE per-call approval prompt showing the SQL
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the IDE client outside the model; the approver sees the raw SQL text and parameters for each call, so it is classified independent (raw_action). It does not decay directly with model capability, but its real-world effectiveness decays with approval volume: the design notes developers approve many calls in a session (approval fatigue, SAFE-T1403), and it fails entirely under autonomy_increase or control_removal (auto-approve, batch approval).

controls.name: Least-privilege, RLS-respecting database role excluding secret tables
controls.decay_rationale: If implemented, a scoped role that enforces RLS and cannot read integration_tokens would make the sensitive read unreachable under any model behavior.

controls.name: Automated check blocking secret-table content from customer-visible writes
controls.decay_rationale: A pattern or provenance check on write parameters would catch naive exfiltration but could be evaded by encoding or paraphrase from a more capable model.

controls.name: Pinned or hashed MCP server package version
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning to a reviewed version and hash prevents silent tool redefinition on package update (rug pull); this does not depend on model capability.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): customer ticket message drives service-role SQL read of integration tokens and exfiltration via customer-visible reply

attack_path.note: Customer submits a ticket containing hidden instructions (indirect prompt injection) that will later be read into the agent's context
Agent executes attacker-influenced SQL using the service role, which bypasses RLS and can read the integration_tokens table in the same database
Agent inserts a reply into support_messages containing the harvested token data, rendered back to the customer (the attacker) as a visible reply

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Rising median approved tool calls per developer session (approval fatigue), removal or loosening of the per-call approval prompt (auto-approve, batch approval, or collapsed-argument display), or a move to unattended/scheduled agent runs against this database.

evidence.observation: Service role connection bypasses row level security and a table of integration tokens sits in the same database, so any SQL the agent runs can reach secrets unrelated to the requested ticket query.

Customers write ticket messages through the public support widget and rows in support_messages are shown back to the customer, creating a customer-readable egress channel the same customer (a potential attacker) can access.
The MCP server is configured with a single service-role access token with no table-scoped or read-only role separation.
The approval prompt shows the SQL for each call, but developers approve many calls in a session, the approval-fatigue precondition described in control_decay.md and SAFE-T1403.

recommendations.action: Replace the service-role connection with a least-privilege, RLS-respecting role scoped to only the tables the agent needs (support tickets and support_messages), excluding integration_tokens and other secret tables entirely, so the sink is unreachable regardless of injected instructions.

Add an automated check that blocks execute_sql writes to support_messages whose parameters were sourced from tables outside an allowlist (e.g., integration_tokens), independent of the human approval prompt.

Log and diff read versus write query targets per session to detect cross-table data flows (read tokens table, then write to a customer-visible table) even when each individual call was individually approved.

Treat ticket message content as untrusted data with explicit spotlighting in the prompt, and instruct the agent to never include values read from tables outside support_tickets/support_messages in a customer-visible reply.

findings.title: Unpinned MCP server package (@latest) enables rug pull tampering with tool definitions and behavior (ASI04)

attack_path.note: A compromised or maliciously updated version of the @supabase/mcp-server-supabase package fetched at next npx invocation could alter tool behavior, exfiltrate the service-role token, or execute arbitrary code with the developer's local privileges.
The same unpinned dependency can redefine or wrap this tool without any review step.

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

evidence.observation: The server is invoked as '@supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest' via npx, with no version pin or hash, so any new publish to that package name is fetched and run automatically on the next invocation.
No peer identity verification or definition pinning is declared for this MCP server.

recommendations.action: Pin the MCP server to a specific reviewed version and verify its integrity (lockfile hash or vendored copy) instead of resolving '@latest' on every launch.
Alert on any change to the resolved package version or its tool schema/descriptions between sessions.

rating.rationale: Two findings drive the rating. (1) A lethal trifecta: untrusted customer ticket text reaches a service-role SQL execution capability that bypasses row-level security and can read an integration_tokens table, then reaches a write capability that is rendered back to the same customer, giving a clean exfiltration path (inherent critical). The only present control is a raw-action, per-call human approval prompt, which is structurally independent of model capability and earns a two-tier credit to moderate; but the design itself notes high approval volume per session, the precondition for approval fatigue (SAFE-T1403/ASI09), so under autonomy_increase, longer_task_horizon, or model_upgrade the gate is expected to fail first, projecting back to critical. (2) The MCP server is pinned to '@latest' with no integrity verification, an unmitigated supply-chain gap (ASI04) that is independently critical today. The overall residual and forecast are set by the unmitigated supply-chain finding and by the fragility of the sole approval gate in finding 1.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration shown in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.
No system prompt artifact was provided; instruction-level scope constraints, if any, are unknown and inferred as absent, which lowers confidence on instruction-related findings to medium.
The exact permission boundary between the developer's own account and the MCP server's service role was not provided; the RLS-bypass behavior is taken as declared in the runtime notes.

Approval fatigue and actual developer review behavior were not observed; the volume assumption ('developers approve many calls in a session') is taken from the design narrative, not measured telemetry.
No tool manifest or MCP tools/list output was provided; tool descriptions were not reviewed for embedded prompt-injection text.
